question:
A credit analyst on the private credit desk of a Chinese commercial bank is preparing training notes, for a CNY 2 billion private markets program, on how private equity and private debt investments can be structured. The notes contain four statements.

I. Preferred shares in a private company can be negotiated to include specific rights and protections, so their features differ from deal to deal.

II. Convertible private debt provides downside protection through its debt component and upside potential through the option to convert into equity.

III. Private debt can be arranged with senior, subordinate or junior rights, each giving a different level of priority over other creditors.

IV. Preferred shares in private companies all confer the same standard level of influence, and this uniformity is what distinguishes them from common shares.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I and III only
options.C: II, III and IV only
options.D: I, II and III only

solution:
Chinese bank’s credit analyst identifies correct statements on private equity and private debt security forms.

**Concept and theory**

Beyond choosing a structure, the investor chooses the security inside it. Schweser closes the LO section with two short paragraphs:

- Private equity can be common shares or preferred shares. Preferred shares “can be negotiated to include specific rights and protections”; as a result, “not all preferred shares offer the same features or level of influence”. In private markets, terms are bargained deal by deal rather than standardized.
- Private debt can be convertible or nonconvertible, with varying seniority. Convertible debt gives downside protection through its debt component and upside potential through the option to convert into equity. Debt can be organized with senior, subordinate or junior rights, each giving a different priority over other creditors.

The idea that unifies both paragraphs is customization: because the securities are privately negotiated, their rights depend on the bargain struck, which is the same theme as the structures themselves.

question: A supervisor at a European securities regulator is reviewing a fund distributor’s marketing brochure, which compares private market structures for clients with EUR 5 million or more to invest. Which of the following comparisons in the brochure is most accurate?

question:
A senior risk analyst at a Singapore sovereign wealth fund is validating the deal-level performance a general partner reports for one buyout. The fund’s cash flows for the deal (SGD million, end of year, negative values are investments by the fund) are shown below, together with two other items from the GP’s deal sheet.

| Item | Year Cash flow |
|---|---|
| Initial equity investment | 0 −80 |
| Follow-on equity investment | 1 −20 |
| Dividend recapitalization distribution | 3 30 |
| Exit proceeds | 5 150 |
| Entry EV/EBITDA multiple | 9.0x |
| Fund committed capital | SGD 1,200 million |

Which of the following is closest to the internal rate of return (IRR) of this deal?
solution:
Senior risk analyst at a Singapore SWF computes the IRR of a buyout with a follow-on investment, an interim dividend recap and an exit.

**Concept and theory**

The internal rate of return is the single discount rate that sets the net present value of all of an investment’s cash flows to zero. GARP’s performance evaluation chapter (Bodie and Marcus) introduces it as the dollar-weighted rate of return: you equate the present value of cash outflows with the present value of cash inflows and solve for the rate. It is “dollar weighted” because periods in which more capital is at work influence the average more. In private equity the investor does not control when capital is called or returned, so a rate that respects the actual timing of each cash flow is natural, which is why Schweser calls the IRR the most commonly used private equity metric: it is annualized, incorporates the timing of cash flows (time value of money), and is well suited to multi-year projects and to comparing competing investments.

$0 = \sum_{\text{t}=0}^{\text{T}} \frac{\text{CF}_{\text{t}}}{(1 + \text{IRR})^{\text{t}}}$

where $\text{CF}_{\text{t}}$ is the net cash flow at the end of year t (negative for capital invested, positive for distributions) and T is the final year. With more than one sign change or uneven flows there is no closed form; on the exam you use the calculator’s cash-flow worksheet.

question: An internal auditor at a Brazilian insurer is reviewing the limited partnership agreement of a private equity fund to which the insurer has committed BRL 300 million. The general partner earns carried interest only if the fund’s net IRR exceeds 8% per year. The auditor is preparing a list of concerns that arise from the design of the IRR itself. Which of the following concerns is the most accurate?

options.A: Because the IRR assumes interim distributions are reinvested at the risk-free rate, it systematically understates the fund’s performance relative to the hurdle.
options.B: Because the IRR measures performance against an explicit public market benchmark, the GP has an incentive to hold portfolios that track that benchmark.
options.C: Because the IRR is computed on committed rather than deployed capital, the GP has an incentive to call the full commitment as early as possible.
options.D: Because the IRR is not adjusted for risk, an IRR-based carry hurdle can give the GP an incentive to pursue riskier deals to clear the hurdle.

solution:
Brazilian insurer’s internal auditor lists concerns that arise from a carry hurdle based on the fund’s net IRR.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser lists the IRR’s advantages (intuitive, incorporates time value of money, widely accepted) and six disadvantages:

| IRR disadvantage (source) | What it means in practice |
|---|---|
| Not adjusted for risk | Can incentivize managers to pursue riskier deals |
| Highly sensitive to cash-flow timing | Potential for manipulation; short-term bias |
| Assumes reinvestment at the IRR | Interim cash assumed to earn the IRR itself |
| Credit lines accelerate distributions | Shorter holding period, overstated IRR |
| No explicit benchmark or market context | Cannot say if the manager beat the market |
| Measures only deployed capital | Ignores cash drag of uncalled commitments |

The point of the first row is incentives. A number that rewards return but never charges for risk invites the decision maker to take more risk: a riskier deal with a higher expected IRR looks strictly better.

**Applying it to this question**

The GP’s carried interest depends on clearing an 8% IRR. The IRR does not penalize risk, so taking riskier deals raises the chance of clearing the hurdle without any offsetting charge in the metric. This is the concern that follows directly from the IRR’s design. The BRL 300 million commitment is context only.

options.A: DPI 0.44x, RVPI 0.76x, TVPI 1.20x

DPI $= \frac{\text{cumulative distributions}}{\text{capital called}} \text{RVPI} = \frac{\text{residual value (NAV)}}{\text{capital called}}$

DPI = 22/40 = 0.55x

TVPI = (22 + 38)/40 = 1.50x = 0.55 + 0.95

question: A treasury analyst at an Australian superannuation fund is presenting the submetrics of the multiple of invested capital (MOIC) to newly hired analysts who will monitor the fund’s AUD private equity commitments. Which of the following statements best describes these submetrics?

options.A: DPI relies entirely on realized cash flows, so it is not subject to valuation manipulation and is often preferred once a fund has generated sufficient realizations, although realized flows may reflect conditions that differ from those affecting the unrealized assets.
options.B: RVPI naturally falls as a fund invests in assets that appreciate in value, so a rising RVPI during the investment period is a direct sign that residual values are being overstated.
options.C: TVPI, as the primary MOIC measure, is not subject to valuation manipulation, because it is anchored on capital called rather than on the manager’s estimate of residual value.
options.D: DPI is the preferred measure throughout a fund’s life, including the early investment period, because realized cash flows cannot be manipulated by the manager.

solution:
Australian super fund’s treasury analyst explains the MOIC submetrics to new analysts.

**Concept and theory**

The three submetrics differ in how much of them rests on the manager’s own valuation:

| Metric | Basis | Property stated in Schweser |
|---|---|---|
| DPI | Realized cash only | Not subject to valuation manipulation; often preferred when sufficient realizations have occurred; limitation: realized flows may reflect conditions that differ from those affecting remaining assets |
| RVPI | Residual value (NAV) | Naturally increases as the fund invests in assets that appreciate; can be manipulated if residual values are overstated |
| TVPI | DPI + RVPI | Primary MOIC measure; can be manipulated if managers inflate valuations, because it includes residual value |

Intuition: cash that has come back is a fact; a valuation is an opinion. But early in a fund’s life there is little cash back, so DPI tells you little, and the exits that have happened may have occurred in a different market from the one the remaining assets face.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option makes a claim about one submetric. Check each against the table: only A matches all three DPI facts (realized basis, no valuation manipulation, preferred once sufficient realizations exist, and its limitation).

question:
A portfolio manager at a UK university endowment compares two fully realized buyout deals made by the same manager. Each deal had a single investment and a single exit (GBP million).

| Deal | Invested (Year 0) | Exit year | Exit proceeds | Entry EV/EBITDA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P | 40 | 2 | 72 | 8.5 |
| Q | 40 | 7 | 112 | 10.0 |

Which of the following statements is the most accurate?

options.A: The IRRs are about 40.0% for P and 25.7% for Q; the IRR ranks P above Q while MOIC ranks Q above P, because MOIC ignores the holding period.
options.B: The IRRs are about 34.2% for P and 15.8% for Q; the IRR ranks P above Q while MOIC ranks Q above P, because MOIC ignores the holding period.
options.C: The IRRs are about 34.2% for P and 15.8% for Q; Q’s higher MOIC shows that Q delivered the better risk-adjusted outcome, so the IRR ranking should be overridden.
options.D: The IRRs are about 29.4% for P and 14.7% for Q; the IRR ranks P above Q while MOIC ranks Q above P, because MOIC ignores the holding period.

The IRR and MOIC answer different questions. MOIC asks “how much?” (value per unit invested, ignoring time). IRR asks “how fast?” (annualized rate incorporating the timing of cash flows). When holding periods differ, they can rank the same two deals in opposite order. For a deal with one investment $\text{C}_{0}$ at time 0 and one exit $\text{V}_{\text{T}}$ at year T, the two are linked by:

MOIC $= \frac{\text{V}_{\text{T}}}{\text{C}_{0}}$ , IRR $= \text{MOIC}^{\text{1/T}} -$ 1

where T is the holding period in years. This link exists only because the timing is known; MOIC by itself cannot be annualized. Neither metric is adjusted for risk.

**Applying it to this question**

Entry EV/EBITDA multiples are irrelevant.

$\text{MOIC}_{\text{P}} =$ 72/40 = 1.80x $\text{MOIC}_{\text{Q}} =$ 112/40 = 2.80x

$\text{IRR}_{\text{P}} =$ $\text{1.80}^{\text{1/2}} -$ 1 = 1.3416 − 1 = 34.2% $\text{IRR}_{\text{Q}} =$ $\text{2.80}^{\text{1/7}} -$ 1 = 1.1585 − 1 = 15.8%

Check: 40 × $\text{1.3416}^{2} =$ 72.0 40 × $\text{1.1585}^{7} =$ 112.0

IRR ranks P first (34.2% vs 15.8%); MOIC ranks Q first (2.8x vs 1.8x). The reversal arises because Q held capital for seven years: MOIC ignores the holding period, while the IRR reflects it.

A risk consultant is advising a US family office that is a limited partner in a buyout fund. For one deal, the limited partner’s cash flows (USD million, end of year) would be as follows without a subscription credit facility. With the facility, the GP funds the acquisition at Year 0 by drawing on the facility and calls the limited partner’s USD 100 million only at the end of Year 1; the distributions are unchanged. Ignore interest and fees on the facility.

| Year | Without facility | With facility |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | −100 | 0 |
| 1 | 0 | −100 |
| 2 | 40 | 40 |
| 5 | 140 | 140 |

Which of the following best describes the effect of the facility on the limited partner’s reported performance for this deal?

options.A: IRR rises from about 16.0% to 20.0%; MOIC is unchanged at 1.80x; the rise reflects a shorter measured holding period.
options.B: IRR falls from about 20.3% to 15.0%; MOIC is unchanged at 1.80x; the facility lengthens the measured holding period.
options.C: IRR rises from about 15.0% to 20.3%; MOIC is unchanged at 1.80x; the rise shows that the GP has created additional value for the limited partner.

A subscription credit facility lets the GP buy assets with borrowed money and call limited partners’ capital later. From the LP’s side, the capital goes out later while the distributions arrive on the same dates, so the LP’s capital is measured as outstanding for a shorter period. Schweser: managers may delay capital calls by drawing on credit lines, which shortens holding periods and can artificially boost reported IRRs; the IRR “can overstate performance when credit lines are used to accelerate distributions”. MOIC is unaffected because it ignores timing: the same 100 produces the same 180. Facility interest is ignored here, as the stem instructs, so the effect isolates the timing.

$0 = \sum_{\text{t}} \frac{\text{CF}_{\text{t}}}{(1 + \text{r})^{\text{t}}}, \qquad \text{MOIC} = \frac{\sum \text{distributions}}{\sum \text{capital invested}}$

UK pension’s three co-investments (GBP 28m to 40m, LBOs and a toll road) dwarf its largest fund look-through exposure (GBP 6m).

**Concept and theory**

A fund commitment spreads each LP’s money across many companies, so the LP’s exposure to any one company is a small slice. A co-investment does the opposite: the investor writes one cheque into one company. Schweser notes that co-investments “are typically larger, more concentrated positions than standard fund exposures”, so portfolios “may become less diversified and more sensitive to deal-specific risks”. It adds that many co-investments involve leveraged buyouts or infrastructure projects, “increasing the risk of unintended concentration”.

Adding positions only diversifies when each position is small relative to the whole. Three large single-deal positions on top of many small look-through slices raise, not lower, deal-specific risk.

**Applying it to this question**

Compare sizes: the largest single-company exposure through all 14 funds is GBP 6 million; the co-investments are GBP 35, 28 and 40 million, roughly 4.7 to 6.7 times larger:

$\frac{28}{6} \approx$ 4.7, $\frac{40}{6} \approx$ 6.7.
